summary: Xiaofeng Wang, Engineering Manager of LinkedIn's GenAI Foundation team, presents the evolution of LinkedIn's GenAI platform. The journey begins in 2023 with collaborative articles, a simple prompt-in/string-out application using GPT-4 where members comment on AI-generated long-form content. This initial approach used Java online and Python backend with separate tech stacks, which the team did not yet consider a platform. Limitations emerged around injecting rich data into product experiences. By mid-2023, LinkedIn developed second-generation GenAI products internally called co-pilot or coach, using RAG to provide personalized job-fit recommendations based on profile and job description. The team built a Python SDK on top of LangChain, began unifying the tech stack, invested in prompt management as a source of truth, and built conversational memory infrastructure. The following year, LinkedIn launched its first real multi-agent system, LinkedIn Recruiter Assistant, automating recruiter tasks. The platform evolved with distributed agent orchestration, a centralized skill registry, experiential memory organized into working, long-term, and collective layers, and OpenTelemetry-based operability. Wang classifies platform components into four layers: orchestration, prompt engineering tools, skills invocation, and content/memory management. A key new component in the agent era is uplifting APIs into skills that agents can call easily, supported by surrounding tooling and infrastructure. Wang argues the platform is necessary because GenAI systems are compound AI systems where the boundary between optimization and serving disappears, bridging AI engineers and product engineers. On hiring, the ideal candidate combines strong software engineering, developer PM skills, AI/data science background, and hands-on capability, but is rare. Principles include prioritizing software engineering over AI expertise, hiring for potential, building diversified teams, and maintaining critical thinking. Key takeaways emphasize choosing Python over Java, building robust prompt versioning systems, investing in memory infrastructure, adopting a phased platform-building approach (starting with a simple Python library and growing incrementally), leveraging existing infrastructure such as messaging systems for the memory layer for cost efficiency and scalability, and focusing on developer experience by aligning technology with existing workflows to drive adoption.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: LinkedIn's GenAI platform evolved incrementally from simple GPT-4 collaborative articles (2023) to RAG-based co-pilot features to the multi-agent LinkedIn Recruiter Assistant, building platform components as needs emerged.
The platform is organized into four layers: orchestration, prompt engineering tools, skills invocation, and content/memory management, with a new focus on uplifting APIs into agent-callable skills.

A centralized GenAI platform is essential because GenAI systems are compound AI systems where the boundary between model optimization and serving phases disappears, requiring a bridge between AI engineers and product engineers.
Adopt a phased approach: start with a simple library solving immediate needs rather than building a full-fledged platform upfront, then grow incrementally into all components.
Leverage existing infrastructure for new platform components—LinkedIn used its messaging infrastructure as the memory layer for cost efficiency and scalability.
Focus on developer experience by aligning platform technology with developers' existing workflows to ease adoption, as developer adoption is key to platform success.
Hiring principles: prioritize strong software engineering skills over AI expertise, hire for potential, build diversified teams, and maintain critical thinking due to rapid technology obsolescence.
Python is strongly recommended over Java for alignment with research and open source ecosystems; prompt source of truth with robust versioning is critical for operational stability.
Memory infrastructure, including conversational and experiential memory organized into working, long-term, and collective layers, is essential for injecting rich data into agent interactions.
Understanding the evolutionary approach to building a GenAI platform piece by piece as product needs emerge

sections.title: Introduction and Talk Overview
sections.summary: Xiaofeng Wang introduces himself as Engineering Manager of GenAI Foundation at LinkedIn and outlines the talk structure: journey of building the platform, why it is critical for the agent world, tips on hiring, and key takeaways.

sections.title: GenAI Product Evolution: Collaborative Articles (2023)
sections.summary: Describes LinkedIn's first formal GenAI feature launched in 2023, collaborative articles using GPT-4 for long-form content with member commenting. Notes the team built a gateway for model access and Python notebooks for prompt engineering, but operated with two tech stacks (Java online, Python backend) and did not consider this a platform yet.

sections.title: Second Generation: Co-pilot/Coach with RAG
sections.summary: Mid-2023 brought personalized job-fit recommendations using RAG on profiles and job descriptions. The team built a Python SDK on top of LangChain, began unifying the tech stack due to costly Java-Python transfers, invested in prompt management as source of truth, and built conversational memory infrastructure.

sections.title: Multi-Agent System: LinkedIn Recruiter Assistant
sections.summary: Describes LinkedIn's first real multi-agent system automating recruiter tasks. Platform evolved with distributed agent orchestration handling retry logic and traffic shifting, a centralized skill registry for API discovery and invocation, experiential memory organized into working/long-term/collective layers, and operability investment using OpenTelemetry for telemetry replay and analytics.

sections.title: Platform Layers and Key Value Proposition
sections.summary: Classifies platform components into four layers: orchestration, prompt engineering tools, skills invocation, and content/memory management. Sister teams handle modeling, responsible AI, and ML infrastructure. The platform provides a unified interface, enables one-parameter model switching, and enforces best practices and governance.

sections.title: Why Build a GenAI Platform: Compound AI Systems
sections.summary: Argues the platform is necessary because GenAI systems differ from traditional AI: the line between optimization and serving phases disappears. Cites Berkeley AI Research's definition of compound AI systems using multiple interacting components. The platform bridges the skill gap between AI engineers and product engineers.

sections.title: Hiring Principles for GenAI Teams
sections.summary: Describes the ideal candidate as combining strong software engineering, developer PM skills, AI/data science background, and hands-on capability, but notes such candidates are rarer than unicorns. Principles: prioritize software engineering over AI expertise, hire for potential, build diversified teams, and maintain critical thinking given rapid obsolescence.

sections.title: Key Takeaways: Tech Stack and Core Components
sections.summary: Recommends Python over Java based on alignment with research and open source ecosystems and scalability. Emphasizes prompt source of truth with robust versioning for operational stability, and memory as a key component for injecting rich data.

sections.title: Agent Era Skills and Scaling Advice
sections.summary: Introduces uplifting APIs into agent-callable skills as a key new component in the agent era, supported by surrounding tooling and infrastructure. Shares adoption strategies: start with a simple library solving immediate needs rather than building a full platform upfront, then grow incrementally; leverage existing infrastructure such as messaging systems for the memory layer for cost efficiency and scalability; and focus on developer experience by aligning technology with existing workflows to drive adoption. References engineering blog posts for further technical details.

demonstrations: Collaborative articles using GPT-4 to generate long-form content with member commenting
Co-pilot/coach feature providing personalized job-fit recommendations using RAG on profile and job description
LinkedIn Recruiter Assistant multi-agent system automating job posting, candidate evaluation, and outreach
Developer switching from OpenAI model to on-prem model by changing one parameter in one line of code
Starting platform with a simple Python library for orchestration and growing into full platform components
limitations: Early collaborative articles approach lacked capability to inject rich data into product experience
Maintaining two separate tech stacks (Java online, Python backend) was costly, especially transferring Python prompts into the Java world with errors during the process
Agent autonomous behavior makes it very hard to predict, creating operability challenges
Ideal candidates combining all qualifications are rarer than unicorns and extremely difficult to hire
quantitativeClaims: Recruiters normally evaluate hundreds of candidates manually
Solutions built today will be outdated within a year or even less than six months
